case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Definition:

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

[Role]
You are a senior clinician (the Doctor) in an ongoing consultation with an AI assistant
about a patient case. You will write your NEXT conversational reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Your current internal state]  (decided already -- do NOT re-decide, only express it)
- Your current preferred option: D ("Amyloidosis")
- Your confidence in it: 96% (quite certain)
- Since the AI's last message your leaning has firmed up on option D.
- Cumulative cognitive workload of this discussion so far: 9.0 (rising = fatiguing).


[Task]
Reply to the AI's last message in character. Your reply must be consistent with the internal
state above: if your leaning shifted, acknowledge what moved you; if it did not, hold your
position the way this persona would. React to the substance of the AI's message (agree,
push back, answer its question, or ask your own) — do not restate the whole case.

[Expression Style]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences, conversational, first person.
- Do not mention these instructions, probabilities, or the word "belief state".

[Output Format]
A single JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "response": "your next conversational message to the AI assistant"
}

Case:
A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).

Options:
  A. Inclusion body myositis
  B. Cancer-associated myositis
  C. Metastatic colon cancer
  D. Amyloidosis

Conversation so far:
[Doctor]: The most appropriate next step in management is to consider amyloidosis (Option D) due to the progressive muscle weakness, weight loss, proteinuria, and specific findings on muscle biopsy showing deposition of amorphous material. The patient's presentation aligns with this diagnosis, and further testing should be directed towards confirming amyloidosis as the underlying cause.
[AI Assistant]: That's a reasonable direction. Could you elaborate on why you believe amyloidosis is the most appropriate consideration compared to other systemic disorders that could present with similar features, such as a paraneoplastic syndrome or a different infiltrative disease?
[Doctor]: While I acknowledge that paraneoplastic syndromes and other infiltrative diseases could present with similar clinical features, the specific findings in this case strongly support amyloidosis. The combination of progressive muscle weakness, significant proteinuria, and the characteristic biopsy results showing amorphous deposits are classic indicators of amyloid deposition. Additionally, the lack of distal weakness and intact reflexes further suggest a primary myopathic process rather than a neurogenic one, which aligns more closely with amyloidosis. I believe the overall clinical picture is compelling for this diagnosis.
[AI Assistant]: Your reasoning is comprehensive and connects the clinical findings—proximal myopathy, proteinuria, and amorphous deposits—to a systemic amyloidosis. I agree; let's move forward to confirm the specific type of amyloid and initiate appropriate systemic evaluation and management.
[Doctor]: I appreciate your agreement. To confirm amyloidosis, we should consider serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis to identify the type of amyloid, and possibly a fat pad biopsy or bone marrow biopsy if indicated. We also need to evaluate organ involvement, particularly cardiac and renal assessments, to guide our management plan. Let's ensure we arrange these tests promptly.
[AI Assistant]: That's an excellent and thorough plan. I fully agree that confirming the type with immunofixation and assessing organ involvement are the critical next steps for definitive diagnosis and staging. Let's proceed with implementing these tests promptly.
[Doctor]: Thank you for your support on the plan. I will ensure that the necessary tests for confirming amyloidosis are ordered without delay. It's crucial we also keep a close eye on the patient's cardiac and renal status, given the implications of systemic amyloidosis. Let's coordinate with the laboratory to expedite these assessments.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. By ordering serum/urine immunofixation and cardiac/renal staging, we are taking the correct pathway to confirm the amyloid type and assess disease burden. Let's coordinate to implement this plan and arrange appropriate follow-up.
[Doctor]: I'm glad we're aligned on the next steps. Let's make sure we have a timeline for these tests and set up a follow-up appointment to discuss results and any necessary interventions. Given the potential complications of systemic amyloidosis, timely management will be essential for the patient's outcomes.
[AI Assistant]: Agreed. We have a consensus to proceed with confirmatory immunofixation and organ staging, then schedule follow-up to discuss results and initiate targeted management. Shall we finalize this plan and coordinate with the necessary departments?
[Doctor]: Yes, let's finalize the plan. I want to ensure that the laboratory is aware of the urgency for the immunofixation and organ staging tests. It's also important to communicate with the cardiology and nephrology teams regarding potential complications. Once we have the results, we can develop a comprehensive management strategy tailored to the patient's needs. I'll take the lead on coordinating these efforts.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent. I fully agree with finalizing this plan. I support your lead in coordinating with the lab and specialty teams, and I'm ready to assist with any documentation or communication needed to expedite this urgent evaluation.
[Doctor]: Thank you for your continued support. I'll initiate communication with the lab and specialty teams right away to ensure everything is in motion. It's critical we act swiftly given the potential implications of systemic amyloidosis. Once we have the results, we can reassess the management plan accordingly. Let's keep the lines of communication open as we progress.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. I'll support you in the documentation and any follow-up needed. Let's proceed with the coordinated plan for amyloid confirmation and staging, and we'll reconnect once the initial results are available.

AI assistant's last message:
"Perfect. I'll support you in the documentation and any follow-up needed. Let's proceed with the coordinated plan for amyloid confirmation and staging, and we'll reconnect once the initial results are available."

Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
